name: Valproic acid topical spray

card.summary: A topical form of valproic acid, a drug that inhibits GSK-3beta and is studied as a way to stimulate hair regrowth in androgenetic alopecia, aimed at restoring density and hairline.
card.note: Valproic acid is a prescription anticonvulsant with serious systemic risks; the topical hair use is investigational and not an approved product.

quick.overview:
Valproic acid is a long-established anticonvulsant and mood-stabilizing drug. Researchers noticed it inhibits glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta (GSK-3beta), part of the Wnt signaling pathway involved in the hair growth cycle, and have tested it on the scalp in a spray form as a possible hair-regrowth treatment.
The appearance goal is thicker hair on thinning scalps. Evidence is early: a 2012 study reported hair regeneration in mice and activity in human dermal papilla cells, and a 2014 randomized, comparative feasibility study in men with androgenetic alopecia reported increased hair count using phototrichogram analysis.
quick.how: Topical valproate has appeared in research settings as a spray applied to the scalp. It is not a standard commercial hair product, and discussion of it is mostly in the research literature and among people following experimental hair-loss approaches. Studies of related delivery systems such as microneedles and nanocarriers are also reported.
quick.risks: Taken by mouth, valproic acid is a prescription drug with significant warnings, including birth defects when used in pregnancy, and hair abnormalities are among its reported effects. Topical use is investigational, and its safety profile for long-term scalp use has not been established in published trials.

lead: Valproic acid (VPA) is a prescription medicine used for epilepsy and bipolar disorder. In hair research, VPA has attracted interest because it inhibits GSK-3beta, which relates to Wnt signaling in the hair follicle. A 2012 PLoS One paper reported that valproic acid induced hair regeneration in a mouse model and activated alkaline phosphatase activity in human dermal papilla cells [1].

A topical spray form has been tested in people. A 2014 Journal of Dermatology study titled 'Topical valproic acid increases the hair count in male patients with androgenetic alopecia' described a randomized, comparative clinical feasibility study using phototrichogram analysis [2]. Later work has explored other delivery methods: dissolving microneedles loaded with valproic acid (2018) [3] and a valproate-choline ionic liquid for transdermal delivery (2025) [4], and a 2024 randomized study compared topical sodium valproate nanospanlastics with topical steroid for alopecia areata [5].

The topic is niche: published human data are limited to small early studies, and no topical valproic acid spray is an approved hair-loss medicine. Hair abnormalities have also been described as an effect of oral valproate, which researchers have reviewed separately [6].

chain: Inhibits GSK-3beta and may activate Wnt signaling in follicles
May increase hair count in androgenetic alopecia
angle.text: The idea is that a topical GSK-3beta inhibitor could thicken thinning hair by acting on follicle signaling. Early studies report increased hair counts, but the approach remains investigational.

infobox: Mouse and cell study 2012; human feasibility study 2014

paras: VPA's proposed role in hair growth is tied to GSK-3beta inhibition and activation of Wnt signaling, which are associated with dermal papilla cells in the follicle. The 2012 study reported that VPA induced hair regeneration in mice and increased alkaline phosphatase activity, a marker linked to dermal papilla function, in human dermal papilla cells [1].

A 2014 randomized, comparative clinical feasibility study in male patients with androgenetic alopecia, using phototrichogram analysis, reported that topical valproic acid increased hair count [2]. Related studies have tested other delivery routes: a 2024 randomized controlled study compared topical sodium valproate nanospanlastics with conventional steroid therapy in alopecia areata [5]. Preclinical delivery work includes dissolving microneedles loaded with valproic acid [3] and a valproate-choline ionic liquid [4]. Studies are small, and no large phase 3 trials are listed.

Oral valproate is associated with a range of adverse effects, including hair abnormalities, and a 2022 review discussed the pathophysiology and management of valproate-associated hair changes [6]. Topical formulations are intended to limit systemic exposure, but long-term safety of scalp use has not been established in published trials.
